title: Khanates and the Russian Conquest
subtitle: 1747–1828 · Erekle II and Georgievsk, the Khanates of the Kura and Araxes, Gulistan and Turkmenchay

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Erekle II and Solomon I, the khans of Karabakh, Erivan, Sheki, Quba and Baku, the Armenian meliks and the first Russian governors

entries.label: Teimuraz II and Erekle II
entries.hint: Nader Shah confirmed Teimuraz II in Kartli and his son Erekle II in Kakheti in 1744, a recognition of loyal Georgians; Erekle II, who became king of both in 1762 on his father's death, ruled as the leading Caucasian statesman for thirty-six years, a general, builder and diplomat, who tried to bring his kingdom under Russia's protection while resisting Persian and Ottoman pressure.
entries.note: Vakhushti, Description of the Georgian Kingdom; Stephen Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003); Ronald Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation (1994).

entries.label: Solomon I of Imereti
entries.hint: Solomon I, king of Imereti in the west, a vassal of the Ottomans and with strong feudal opposition, expelled the Ottoman garrisons in the 1750s, defeated the Turks at Khresili in 1757, and with Russian help at Aspindza in 1770 against the Ottoman power, though he could not unite the lands of western Georgia, and died in exile in 1784.

entries.label: Giorgi XII, the last king
entries.hint: Erekle's son Giorgi XII, a sick man in an age of dynastic quarrels between his many half-brothers and sons, signed in 1799 the will in which he asked to transfer the crown to Russia, and died on 28 December 1800 as the last king of Kartli–Kakheti.

entries.label: The meliks and the khans of Karabakh
entries.hint: After Nader Shah's death Panah Ali Khan, a Turkic chief of the Javanshir, built the fortress of Shusha in 1750–1752 and made himself ruler of Karabakh; the five Armenian meliks first fought, then served him. His son Ibrahim Khalil Khan (1763–1806) held the khanate against Persia, and signed with Russia in 1805.
entries.note: Mirza Jamal Javanshir, History of Karabagh (1847); Mirza Adigozal-bek, Karabakhname; Robert Hewsen, 'The Meliks of Eastern Armenia' (1972–).

entries.label: Etchmiadzin and the Armenian leaders
entries.hint: The catholicosate, with an Ottoman and Persian confirmation, was held by Simeon of Erevan (1763–1780) and Ephrem I (1809–1830), while the archbishop Nerses of Ashtarak, who led the Armenian volunteers of 1826–1828 against Persia; the church, after Russia took Erivan, became the central institution of the Armenian people of the Caucasus.
entries.note: Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001); George Bournoutian, A Concise History of the Armenian People (2002).

entries.label: The khanates of Erivan, Nakhchivan and Ganja
entries.hint: In place of the Safavid provinces, local Turkic dynasties emerged: the Qajar Khans of Erivan (Hussein Ali Khan, Hussein Khan Sardar), the Kangarlu khans of Nakhchivan, Javad Khan of the Ziyadoghlu at Ganja, the house of Panah Ali Khan at Karabakh and others, each with its own fortress, cavalry and tribute, and the Persian Qajar shah as nominal sovereign.
entries.note: Bournoutian, The Khanate of Erevan under Qajar Rule (1992); Minorsky, A History of Sharvan and Darband (1958).
keywords: Qajar Khans of Erivan Hussein Ali Khan

entries.label: The khanates of Sheki, Shirvan, Quba and Baku
entries.hint: In the north-east, Haji Chelebi Khan founded the Sheki khanate (1743), Fath Ali Khan of Quba (1758–1789) united Quba, Derbent, Baku and Shirvan for a time in a strong khanate, and the Shirvan khans at Shamakhi and Baku governed the rest; Sheki's palace (1797) and Quba's fortress remain.
entries.note: Minorsky 1958; Audrey Altstadt, The Azerbaijani Turks (1992).

entries.label: Tsitsianov, Yermolov and Paskevich
entries.hint: The Russian military governors, Prince Pavel Tsitsianov (1802–1806), Ivan Gudovich, Alexei Yermolov (1816–1827) and Ivan Paskevich (from 1827), ran the Caucasus from Tbilisi, brought in a harsh military administration and annexed the khanates one by one; Tsitsianov was murdered at Baku in 1806.
entries.note: Moshe Gammer, Muslim Resistance to the Tsar (1994); Suny 1994.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Aspindza, Krtsanisi and the sack of Tbilisi, the sieges of Ganja and Erivan and the two Russo-Persian wars

entries.label: Aspindza
entries.hint: In the Russo-Turkish war of 1768–1774 a small Russian corps under Totleben joined the armies of Erekle II and Solomon I and, at Aspindza on 20 April 1770, defeated a much larger Ottoman army, the first Georgian victory of the new alliance; the Russians withdrew soon after and the Georgians were left alone.

entries.label: The sack of Tbilisi
entries.hint: The Qajar shah Agha Mohammad Khan invaded Georgia in 1795 with some 35,000 men, when Erekle II, who had counted on Russian help under the treaty of Georgievsk, had only a small force; after the battle of Krtsanisi on 8–10 September Tbilisi was taken, burnt and plundered, thousands were killed and some 15,000 captives taken to Persia.

entries.label: Agha Mohammad Khan at Shusha
entries.hint: After Tbilisi, Agha Mohammad Khan besieged Shusha for 33 days in 1795 without taking it, had himself crowned shah in 1796 and in 1797 returned to Shusha, where he was murdered by his own servants on 17 June. The event relieved Karabakh and left the Qajar claim unsettled.
entries.note: Mirza Jamal Javanshir; Gavin Hambly in Cambridge History of Iran, vol. 7 (1991).

entries.label: The first Russo-Persian war
entries.hint: After the annexation of Georgia and the Karabakh khan's submission in 1805, Russian troops stormed Ganja in January 1804, failed to take Erivan in 1804, took Baku in 1806 and Derbent in 1806, and fought Abbas Mirza's army at Aslanduz in 1812; the war ended with the treaty of Gulistan. It was fought alongside the Russo-Turkish war of 1806–1812.
entries.note: Gammer 1994; Hambly 1991; George Bournoutian, Russia and the Armenians of Transcaucasia (1998).

entries.label: The fall of Ganja and Baku
entries.hint: Tsitsianov stormed Ganja in January 1804, killing Javad Khan and thousands of defenders, renamed it Elisavetpol, and in February 1806 both Tsitsianov and the khan Huseyn Quli were killed outside Baku when the khan came to hand over the keys; Bulgakov occupied the city in October.

entries.label: The rising of Kakheti
entries.hint: Georgians of Kakheti and the highlands, resenting Russian taxes, the loss of the monarchy and the abolition of church autonomy, rose in 1812 under Prince Grigol and the heir Alexander, with Persian support, and were put down; earlier risings had occurred in 1802 and 1804, and the discontent led to the conspiracy of 1832.

entries.label: Erivan and the second Russo-Persian war
entries.hint: In 1826 Persian forces under Abbas Mirza invaded the Karabakh and Ganja khanates and were defeated at Shamkir and at Ganja in September; General Paskevich took the fortress of Sardarabad in July 1827 and Erivan on 1 October 1827, and Tabriz fell soon after. The war ended with the treaty of Turkmenchay.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The treaty of Georgievsk, the manifesto of 1801, Gulistan, Turkmenchay and the Armenian Oblast

entries.label: The treaty of Georgievsk
entries.hint: In the treaty of Georgievsk, signed in the Russian fortress on the Caucasus line, Erekle II placed Kartli–Kakheti under the protection of Catherine II, giving up the right to treat with other powers, in return for Russia's guarantee of the kingdom's integrity and the Bagrationi succession; Russia failed to send the troops needed in 1795.

entries.label: The annexation of 1801
entries.hint: The manifesto of Alexander I of 12 September 1801 declared Kartli–Kakheti annexed to the Russian empire, abolished the monarchy and set up a Russian administration under a commander-in-chief; the Georgian princes and the royal family were soon deported to Russia, and in 1810 Imereti, with its king Solomon II, was also annexed.

entries.label: The treaty of Gulistan
entries.hint: In the treaty of Gulistan Persia gave up Karabakh, Ganja, Sheki, Shirvan, Baku, Derbent, Quba, Talysh, Dagestan and Georgia and its dependencies, and renounced the right to a navy on the Caspian, thus ceding to Russia the lands north of the Araxes except Erivan and Nakhchivan.

entries.label: The treaty of Turkmenchay
entries.hint: The treaty of Turkmenchay fixed the border on the Araxes: Persia ceded the khanates of Erivan and Nakhchivan, paid an indemnity of 20 million roubles, gave Russia capitulatory rights and allowed the emigration of Armenians to the Russian side within a year. The border it drew is still in force.

entries.label: The Armenian Oblast
entries.hint: Created by imperial decree on 21 March 1828 from the khanates of Erivan and Nakhchivan, the Armenian Oblast was the first administrative unit under the name Armenia, to be governed by a Russian governor with a mainly military administration; its use of the name, of the people and the church, was a first recognition of Armenians as a distinct unit.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The abolition of Georgian autocephaly, the Armenian Church under Russia and the Shia clergy of the khanates

entries.label: The Shia clergy of the khanates
entries.hint: In the khanates Shia clergy, the mullahs and the sheikh-ul-Islam, ran the courts, mosques and schools of the Turkic and Persian population and kept links with the Iraqi shrine cities and Persia; the Russians confirmed their property and in the 1820s were uneasy about their influence.

entries.label: The end of Georgian autocephaly
entries.hint: In 1811 the Russian Holy Synod abolished the autocephaly of the Georgian church, which had existed since the fifth century, placed it under a Russian exarch and removed the Catholicos Antoni II to Russia; Russians gradually replaced Georgian clergy and the Georgian liturgy was displaced, a loss deeply resented.

entries.label: The Armenian Church under Russia
entries.hint: After the conquest of Erivan the Russian government, which had given the Armenian church protection and revenues, confirmed the Catholicos of Etchmiadzin as head of all Armenians in the empire and took the monastery under its authority; the 'Polozhenie' of 1836 later defined its relations with the state.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Sayat-Nova, Besiki and Vagif, the palace of Sheki and the Georgian painters

entries.label: Sayat-Nova
entries.hint: Harutyun Sayatyan, known as Sayat-Nova ('king of song'), the troubadour of the court of Erekle II, composed songs in Armenian, Georgian and Azerbaijani Turkic, some 220 of which survive in his manuscript (davtar); he became a priest at Haghpat and died in 1795, according to tradition killed during Agha Mohammad Khan's invasion.
entries.note: Sayat-Nova, Davtar (ed. Chopanian 1914); Charles Dowsett, Sayatnova (1974).

entries.label: Besiki and Vagif
entries.hint: The Georgian court poet Besarion Gabashvili, 'Besiki' (1750–1791), brought the lyric to a high point and was exiled in the quarrels around Erekle's court; Molla Panah Vagif (1717–1797), vizier of the khan of Karabakh and the first great poet of Azerbaijani in simple vernacular forms, was killed in 1797 in the troubles of Agha Mohammad Khan's last campaign.
entries.note: Besiki, Poems; Vagif, Divan; Suny 1994; Altstadt 1992.

entries.label: The palace of the Sheki khans
entries.hint: The summer palace of Sheki, built in 1762 in the style of a mansion with shebeke windows of coloured glass set in a lattice of wood without nails, wall paintings of flowers and hunting scenes and a pair of plane trees, is the best of the khans' buildings; the Sheki fortress and palace are on the UNESCO list (2019).
entries.note: Sheki Khan's Palace (1797); UNESCO World Heritage no. 1549 (2019).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Shahamirian's constitution, Bakikhanov and Javanshir, and the Georgian court's writers

entries.label: The Georgian chroniclers and Vakhushti
entries.hint: Prince Vakhushti Bagrationi, son of Vakhtang VI, wrote in Moscow about 1745 the Description of the Georgian Kingdom, a geography and history of Georgia with maps, the best scholarly work of old Georgia, edited from the older chronicles and from his own observation.
entries.note: Vakhushti Bagrationi, Description of the Georgian Kingdom (1745); Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Shahamirian's constitution
entries.hint: The Armenian merchants of Madras, led by Shahamir Shahamirian and the printer Movses Baghramian, issued in 1773 the 'Snare of Glory' (Vorogayt Parats), a political treatise with a draft constitution for an Armenian republic of citizens, with an elected assembly, in the language of Enlightenment, hoping for liberation from the Persians and Ottomans.
entries.note: Shahamir Shahamirian, Vorogayt Parats (Madras, 1773); Ronald Suny, Looking toward Ararat (1993).

entries.label: Javanshir and Bakikhanov
entries.hint: Mirza Jamal Javanshir (1773–1853) wrote in Persian a History of Karabagh, one of the best accounts of the khanates, and Abbas-Qulu-agha Bakikhanov (1794–1847), a Russian officer from Baku, wrote the Gulistan-i Iram on the history of Shirvan and Dagestan (1841), the first modern history of the region's Muslims.
entries.note: Mirza Jamal Javanshir, History of Karabagh; Bakikhanov, Gulistan-i Iram (1841); Altstadt 1992.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Silk, cotton and oil under the khans, the Georgian Military Road and the Armenian settlement of the Ararat plain

entries.label: Silk, cotton and oil under the khans
entries.hint: The khanates of the Kura plain remained exporters of silk, cotton, rice, fruit and salt, and Baku's oil wells were farmed out to local contractors; the khans taxed the trade with Persia, Russia and the Ottomans, and Russia opened the route from Astrakhan to the Caspian ports.

entries.label: The Armenian migration of 1828
entries.hint: Under the terms of Turkmenchay and Russia's encouragement, some 40,000 Armenians moved from Persian Azerbaijan to the Armenian Oblast in 1828–1830, and 25,000 more from the Ottoman provinces of Erzurum and Bayazid after the war of 1828–1829; Muslims left in numbers, so that Armenians became a majority of the oblast within decades.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Fortresses, artillery and the road through the Darial gorge

entries.label: The Georgian Military Road
entries.hint: A military road from Vladikavkaz over the Darial gorge and the Cross Pass to Tbilisi was begun by the Russians in 1799, opened for wheeled traffic about 1817–1820 and completed in 1863; it linked Russia to Transcaucasia and was the main route of Russian supplies.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Russian diplomacy, Persian and Ottoman wars and the Armenian migration of 1828

entries.label: Georgia between Russia, Persia and the Ottomans
entries.hint: Erekle II and his predecessors had since 1744 manoeuvred among the three empires, accepted Persian suzerainty, sought Russian protection in 1769–1770 and the treaty of 1783, appealed to Austria and Britain; the failure of Russian aid in 1795 and the pressure of the Qajar led the kingdom to annexation.

entries.label: The Russian settlements
entries.hint: The Russian government settled German Württembergers (Katharinenfeld and Helenendorf, from 1818–1819) and later, from the 1830s, Russian sectarians such as the Molokans and Dukhobors, as well as Armenians and Greeks from the Ottoman empire, in the Caucasus, in order to people the frontier and stabilise it, in colonies which later became distinctive towns.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The plague, the sack of Tbilisi and the demographic shift

entries.label: Plague, war and the people
entries.hint: The population of the Caucasus, already reduced by the wars of the eighteenth century, lost heavily in the plague outbreaks of 1800s and 1810s and the wars of 1804–1829, with the sack of Tbilisi in 1795, the sieges and campaigns, and cholera; Russian officials counted about one million in Transcaucasia in the 1830s.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A queen of Georgia, the captives of 1795 and the ashugh of Tbilisi

entries.label: Darejan Dadiani
entries.hint: Darejan, a princess of the Dadiani house of Mingrelia and the last wife of Erekle II, took part in the politics of Kartli–Kakheti, fought for her sons' rights in the succession, resisted the annexation and in 1803 was removed to Russia; she is a main figure in the story of the end of the monarchy.

entries.label: Sayat-Nova's Tbilisi
entries.hint: Tbilisi in Erekle's time was a city of some 20,000 people, Georgians, Armenians and Muslims, with baths, bazaars, craftsmen's guilds (amkari) and the ashughs who sang in the market and at feasts; its Armenian merchants and artisans, who had been the majority, and the rich amkari, were the ones whom the poet sang.

entries.label: The captives of 1795
entries.hint: According to the Georgian chronicle and the Armenian historians, Agha Mohammad Khan's army carried off some 15,000 captives, among them many women and children, from Tbilisi and the countryside; many were sold or settled in Persia, and the loss was remembered in Georgian and Armenian songs.
